record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: Do the envelopes of massive stars inflate when the stellar envelope becomes locally super-Eddington, and how is that inflation altered by rotation? More specifically, can hydrostatic density inversions and envelope inflation inferred in one-dimensional and three-dimensional models be extended to a correct two-dimensional description of rotating stars near the Eddington limit, so that the effect of centrifugal force on the inflation is understood?

evidence.quote: 3.1. Do stellar envelopes inflate near the Eddington limit?
We also need 2D-models of rotating stars near the Eddington limit in order to understand how the centrifugal force affects the envelope inflation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a massive, radiation-dominated star in hydrostatic equilibrium whose radiative luminosity locally approaches or exceeds the Eddington luminosity
L_Edd(r) = 4π G M(r) c / κ(ρ,T),
where κ(ρ,T) is the (Rosseland mean) opacity, M(r) is the mass enclosed within radius r, G is Newton's constant, and c is the speed of light. In one-dimensional stellar-structure calculations of such stars, the iron opacity bump (κ peaking at log T ≈ 5.2) is known to drive a locally super-Eddington layer in the outer envelope that can be reconciled with hydrostatic balance only by introducing a low-density "inflated" extended envelope, often accompanied by a hydrostatic density inversion (dρ/dr > 0). Three-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of non-rotating envelopes confirm that such inflation persists in a turbulent, time-averaged sense.

Now allow the star to rotate with angular velocity Ω(r,θ) (θ being the colatitude), so that in the co-rotating frame the effective gravity includes a centrifugal term −Ω² r sinθ ê_ϖ. Formulate and resolve the following:

(a) Construct a self-consistent two-dimensional model of a rotating massive star in which the radiative flux locally reaches or exceeds the Eddington limit, including realistic opacities (in particular the iron opacity bump), radiative energy transport, and the centrifugal force.

(b) Determine whether, and under what conditions on Ω, M, L, and κ, the envelope inflation and hydrostatic density inversions found in 1D and 3D non-rotating treatments persist in this 2D rotating setting.

(c) Quantify how the centrifugal force modifies the radial extent, density structure, latitudinal dependence, and stability of the inflated envelope, and identify the rotation rate at which inflation is suppressed, enhanced, or rendered gravitationally unbound (mass-shedding) at the equator.
artifact.status_search_result: Envelope inflation near the Eddington limit is established in 1D and 3D non-rotating radiation-hydrodynamic models, and 2D rotating stellar-structure codes such as ESTER have recently been developed. However, fully self-consistent 2D models of rotating massive stars that locally exceed the Eddington limit and quantify the centrifugal modification of envelope inflation are still being developed, and the question is acknowledged as open in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Massive main-sequence stars evolving at the Eddington limit
status_evidence.snippet: Centrifugal force in rapidly rotating stars may lead to similar conditions in the envelope layers near the stellar equator; to compute the effect reliably requires 2D calculations at least.
status_evidence.claim: 2D calculations are required to reliably model the centrifugal effect on envelope inflation, and have not yet been carried out comprehensively.

status_evidence.title: The first two-dimensional stellar structure and evolution models of rotating stars
status_evidence.snippet: ESTER models are 2D models of rotating stars that include the centrifugal distortion of the star.
status_evidence.claim: 2D rotating stellar-structure tools (ESTER) exist but have not yet been applied to fully resolve envelope inflation in super-Eddington rotating massive stars.

status_evidence.title: Stellar envelope inflation near the Eddington limit
status_evidence.snippet: Inflation depends on a dimensionless parameter W related to the Fe-opacity peak topology; for W > 1 the envelope becomes gravitationally unbound.
status_evidence.claim: Inflation is well-characterized in 1D non-rotating models but the rotating 2D extension remains open.
